claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs lines 21-27: `int.Parse(User.FindFirstValue(JwtRegisteredClaimNames.Sub)!)`, `.Select(i => new OrderItem { ... })`, `await orderService.PlaceOrderAsync(customerId, items)`, `return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = order.Id }, ToDto(order));`. Matches the claim exactly.

OrderService.cs:10 `if (items.Count == 0) throw new ArgumentException(...)`; :16 `Status = "new"`; :19-20 `await repository.AddAsync(order); await repository.SaveChangesAsync();`; :21 `notifier.Send(order.Id, "order placed");`; :22 `return order;`.

EF docs: "EF Core creates temporary key values when tracking new entities that will have real key values generated by the database when SaveChanges is called." and "If you create several new related entities, adding one of them to the context will cause the others to be added too." Snapshot: Order.Id UseIdentityByDefaultColumn. So the id claim holds, but Order.Items (order_items rows) are inserted in the same SaveChangesAsync — not a single INSERT/row.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: EfOrderRepository.AddAsync calls db.Orders.AddAsync, which only starts tracking the order and its items; SaveChangesAsync calls db.SaveChangesAsync, which sends the INSERTs for the order and its items. PostgreSQL generates the order's id (identity column) and EF Core sets it on order.Id.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: a count that the code does not support. The Create path touches OrdersController, OrderService, EfOrderRepository, DonHangDbContext and LoggingNotifier (five), plus ExceptionHandlingMiddleware and RequestLoggingMiddleware before the controller. 'Four classes' matches no natural count. 'Three projects' is true (DonHang.Api, DonHang.Domain, DonHang.Infrastructure) but also unlisted.
issues.quote: the request passed through three projects, four classes and a database
issues.fix: Replace with "the request passed through three projects (DonHang.Api, DonHang.Domain, DonHang.Infrastructure), several classes and a database", and add a claim to .meta.json citing the three .csproj files.

issues.text: Unlisted claim, and not true of this app: Program.cs:67-71 runs ExceptionHandlingMiddleware, RequestLoggingMiddleware, CORS, authentication and authorization before MapControllers. The lesson itself relies on this in Try it ("the exception-handling middleware answers 400"), so the trace contradicts itself. The diagram also starts at the controller.
issues.quote: The request enters at the controller.
issues.fix: Write "After passing through the middleware pipeline, the request reaches our own code at the controller." Add a claim citing Program.cs:67-72 @ stage-1.

issues.text: The prose does not match AuthController. Login is a POST that loads a customer, checks the password with PasswordHasher.Verify (from DonHang.Domain), returns 401 on failure and issues a token (AuthController.cs:13-23). That is not a 'simple read with no business rule'. Five-line summary line 4 repeats this.
issues.quote: and the products and login endpoints query `DonHangDbContext` themselves. These are shortcuts for simple reads with no business rule to apply today.
issues.fix: Say that Get, List and the products endpoints are shortcuts for simple reads. Describe login separately: "the login endpoint also queries DonHangDbContext itself, and checks the password in the controller". Fix summary line 4 the same way.

issues.text: Singular INSERT/row is wrong for this entity. Order.Items is a navigation (DonHangDbContext.cs:45), so SaveChangesAsync also inserts one order_items row per item (EF: adding one entity of a new graph adds the related ones). Quiz q1 option a says 'the row' too.
issues.fix: S4: "SaveChangesAsync sends the INSERTs for the order and its items to PostgreSQL". S5: "the moment the rows reach PostgreSQL". q1 option a: "sends the order to PostgreSQL, which assigns the id".

issues.text: At stage-1, INotifier is LoggingNotifier (claim 5), which only writes a log line (LoggingNotifier.cs:11-12). The lesson says a notification is sent, and the situation lists 'a missing notification' as a failure to trace, without saying what 'sent' means here.
issues.quote: The service then sends the "order placed" notification and returns the `Order`.
issues.fix: Write "The service then calls the notifier with 'order placed' (at this stage the notifier only writes a log line) and returns the Order."

issues.text: Summary line 3 states a universal rule that line 4 and section 5 immediately contradict: Get/List call the repository directly and the products/login endpoints call DonHangDbContext directly, so they skip the layer below.
issues.quote: Each layer calls only the one below it, and nothing calls back up.
issues.fix: Write "In `Create`, each layer calls only the one below it, and nothing calls back up."

issues.text: 'Which orders are allowed' is stated without a condition, but section 5 of this lesson says a read rule placed in the service would be skipped by Get. So a rule about which orders may be read does not touch only the service today.
issues.quote: That is why a change to which orders are allowed touches only the service
issues.fix: Write "That is why a change to which orders may be placed touches only the service" (and apply the same wording to summary line 5).

issues.text: The diagram leaves out the notifier call. The prose (S4) and the Try it expected answer both list it as a step of the same request ("→ the notifier's Send →").
issues.fix: Add `S --> N[INotifier.Send]` to the flowchart after the repository edge.

issues.text: The prose says each layer called only the one directly below it, but one of the service's calls goes to INotifier/LoggingNotifier and I am never told which layer that is. I cannot check the 'only the one below' rule for this call, so the claim feels unproven for one of the steps I just read.
issues.quote: Each layer called only the one directly below it, and nothing called back up
issues.fix: In the sentence about the notifier, add a few words saying which project/layer LoggingNotifier lives in (e.g. 'LoggingNotifier, in DonHang.Infrastructure,').

issues.text: Section 4 presents middleware only as the first stop before the controller. Later, Try it says the exception-handling middleware answers 400 after PlaceOrderAsync throws. The step between (the exception passes back up out of Create to the middleware, which wraps the whole request) is never stated, and the situation itself names 'an order refused' as a reason to trace.
issues.quote: The request first passes through the middleware — exception handling, logging, the token check — and then reaches the controller.
issues.fix: Add one sentence at the end of the service paragraph: if the service throws, the exception passes out of Create unhandled and the exception-handling middleware turns it into the response (400 for ArgumentException).

issues.text: In the diagram, C --> A is drawn as a sibling of C --> S, and there are no return arrows, so from the picture alone the 201 could be sent in parallel with the service call. Only the prose ('Back in the controller') tells me it happens after the service returns.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after the diagram saying the arrows show calls going down, and the 201 is built only after PlaceOrderAsync returns to Create.

issues.text: The login sentence stops without saying what it means. The controller-layer lesson told me controllers do not decide business rules, yet here the controller checks the password. Is this a shortcut too, with the same cost? The summary (line 4) and quiz q5 leave login out, so I cannot tell whether it counts.
issues.quote: The login endpoint also queries `DonHangDbContext` itself, and checks the password from the controller with `PasswordHasher` from `DonHang.Domain`.
issues.fix: End the sentence with a short clause saying what this is: e.g. 'another shortcut, and one that already holds a rule (the password check) in the controller'.

issues.text: 'as Get does today' reads as if Get is skipping a service rule right now, but section 5 says there is no read rule today. I had to re-read to see it means 'goes around the service', not 'skips a rule'.
issues.quote: You notice this when a rule you added to the service is silently skipped by a request that went around it, as `Get` does today.
issues.fix: Replace 'as `Get` does today' with 'the way `Get` goes around the service today'.

issues.text: q4 wrong-option explanations confuse me further. Option c's explanation implies Get does not require a signed-in caller, which the lesson never says. Option b's 'would matter when it were about how data is stored' is hard to parse.
issues.quote: A token problem would matter when `Get` required a signed-in caller, but the lesson shows it simply reads through the repository without the rule.
issues.fix: c: 'The customer could open the order, so the token was accepted; the problem is that Get never passes the rule.' b: 'The repository decides how data is stored; "not shown to anyone" is a business rule, so it belongs in the service.'
